claim: Storing temporal sequences of events (i.e., sequence memory) is fundamental to many cognitive functions.
source: Storing temporal sequences of events (i.e., sequence memory) is fundamental to many cognitive functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of sequence memory, supported by established scientific knowledge in cognitive science.

claim: Serially remembered items are successively reactivated during memory retention.
source: We demonstrate that serially remembered items are successively reactivated during memory retention.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from EEG recordings and TRF analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The item-by-item reactivation is compressed within a 200 – 400 ms window.
source: First, the item-by-item reactivation is compressed within a 200 – 400 ms window, suggesting that external events are associated within a plasticity-relevant window to facilitate memory consolidation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the temporal characteristics of neural reactivations.

claim: The replay is in a temporally reversed order.
source: Second, the replay is in a temporally reversed order and is strongly related to the recency effect in behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 showing backward sequential reactivation patterns.

claim: The backward replay is strongly related to the recency effect in behavior.
source: Second, the replay is in a temporally reversed order and is strongly related to the recency effect in behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral analysis showing correlation between backward reactivation and recency effect.

claim: Fast-backward replay has been previously revealed in rat hippocampus.
source: This fast-backward replay, previously revealed in rat hippocampus and demonstrated here in human cortical activities, might constitute a general neural mechanism for sequence memory and learning.
evidence: This claim references established findings from animal studies.

claim: Fast-backward replay might constitute a general neural mechanism for sequence memory and learning.
source: This fast-backward replay, previously revealed in rat hippocampus and demonstrated here in human cortical activities, might constitute a general neural mechanism for sequence memory and learning.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the convergence of findings from rat and human studies.

claim: Sequence memory is crucial to many cognitive functions, including speech recognition, movement planning, and episodic memory.
source: Storing and retrieving temporal sequences of events (i.e., sequence memory), a capacity shared across species, is crucial to many cognitive functions, including speech recognition, movement planning, and episodic memory (Doyon et al., 2003; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neural responses during the retention interval show a sustained load-dependent enhancement.
source: There exists ample evidence that neural responses during the retention interval show a sustained load-dependent enhancement (Buschman et al., 2011; Jensen et al., 2002; Klimesch et al., 1999; Sauseng et al., 2009; Vogel and Machizawa, 2004; Xu and Chun, 2006), suggesting that the maintenance of mnemonic contents is implemented by recurrent feedback loops (Luck and Vogel, 2013), as well as suppression of irrelevant information (Sauseng et al., 2009; Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Maintenance of mnemonic contents is implemented by recurrent feedback loops.
source: There exists ample evidence that neural responses during the retention interval show a sustained load-dependent enhancement (Buschman et al., 2011; Jensen et al., 2002; Klimesch et al., 1999; Sauseng et al., 2009; Vogel and Machizawa, 2004; Xu and Chun, 2006), suggesting that the maintenance of mnemonic contents is implemented by recurrent feedback loops (Luck and Vogel, 2013), as well as suppression of irrelevant information (Sauseng et al., 2009; Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and represents an inference from previous research.

claim: Sequence memory is mediated by a theta-gamma coupled neuronal oscillatory mechanism.
source: Theoretical models postulate that sequence memory is mediated by a theta-gamma coupled neuronal oscillatory mechanism (Jensen and Lisman, 2005; Lisman and Idiart, 1995), such that individual items of the list/sequence, encoded in gamma-band activities, occur at the different phases of a theta-band rhythm.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: A recent MEG study provides evidence supporting the theta-gamma coupling model during the memory encoding period.
source: A recent MEG study provides important evidence supporting this theta-gamma coupling model during the memory encoding period (Heusser et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Place cells in rodent hippocampus fire in the same or reverse order in which they appeared during previous spatial navigation.
source: Despite this gap, it is well-established in animal studies that place cells in rodent hippocampus fire in the same or reverse order in which they appeared during previous spatial navigation, in both awake and asleep status (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Louie and Wilson, 2001; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to animal studies.

claim: Color features have been found to be the type of feature having the strongest conjunction with other features within an object.
source: Most importantly, color features have been found to be the type of feature having the strongest conjunction with other features within an object (Gao et al., 2011; Johnson et al., 2008; Wheeler and Treisman, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: All features of an object, even the task-irrelevant ones, will be stored automatically in working memory.
source: Previous studies have provided evidence supporting the object-based nature of working memory such that all features of an object, even the task-irrelevant ones, will be stored automatically in working memory (Gao et al., 2011; Hollingworth and Luck, 2009; Hyun et al., 2009; Luck and Vogel, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Memory performance in Experiment 1 was well above chance (mean accuracy = 0.888).
source: Eighteen participants participated in Experiment 1, and their memory performance was well above chance (N = 18, mean accuracy = 0.888, s.e. = 0.029; One-sample t-test, df = 17, t = 26.34, p < 0.001, CI: [0.357, 0.419], Cohen's d = 6.208).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The overall TRF response for the color probes showed clear alpha-band patterns and was robust at single-subject level.
source: First, the overall TRF response for the color probes showed clear alpha-band patterns and was robust at single-subject level (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous findings (Jia et al., 2017; VanRullen and Macdonald, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and consistent with previous literature.

claim: Both WM-TRF and NWM-TRF demonstrated clear sustained alpha-band activations (8 – 11 Hz).
source: As shown in Figure 2A, both WM-TRF (left panel) and NWM-TRF (right panel) demonstrated clear sustained alpha-band activations (8 – 11 Hz; permutation test, p < 0.05, corrected, see Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), consistent with previous findings (VanRullen and Macdonald, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and statistical testing.

claim: WM showed significant alpha-band enhancement over NWM from 310 ms to 370 ms.
source: As shown in Figure 2D, WM (red) showed significant alpha-band enhancement over NWM (black) from 310 ms to 370 ms (bootstrap test, p = 0.046, FDR corrected across time), supporting the alpha-band memory effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and statistical testing.

claim: The alpha-mediated memory effects during maintenance could not be interpreted by spatial attention.
source: Thus, the alpha-mediated memory effects during maintenance could not be interpreted by spatial attention.
evidence: This claim is supported by control analyses examining spatial effects.

claim: Task-irrelevant color probes carry memory-related information.
source: Therefore, the observed difference between the WM-TRF and NWM-TRF responses indicates that the task-irrelevant color probes did carry memory-related information, consistent with previous findings advocating the object-based nature of working memory (Gao et al., 2011; Hollingworth and Luck, 2009; Hyun et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and consistent with previous literature.

claim: Significant recency effect (i.e., 2nd item better than 1st item) in behavioral performance was found in Experiment 2.
source: First, significant recency effect (i.e., 2nd item better than 1st item) in behavioral performance was found (N = 19, 1st item: mean = 0.794, s.e. = 0.020; 2nd item: mean = 0.840, s.e = 0.014; recency effect: mean = 0.047, s.e. = 0.020; paired t-test, df = 18, t = 2.378, p = 0.029, CI: [0.005, 0.089], Cohen's d = 0.532).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The 1st-WM-TRF and the 2nd-WM-TRF displayed distinct alpha-band temporal courses.
source: Most interestingly, the 1st-WM-TRF and the 2nd-WM-TRF displayed distinct alpha-band temporal courses (Figure 3C): the 1st-WM-TRF alpha-band response (red line) was temporally delayed by approximately 200 ms relative to that of the 2nd-WM-TRF (blue line) response (alpha-band peak latency, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.036).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and statistical testing.

claim: The 2nd-WM-TRF showed a response at around 80–100 ms, whereas the 1st-WM-TRF showed a response at around 260–300 ms.
source: Specifically, the 2nd-WM-TRF showed a response at around 80–100 ms, whereas the 1st-WM-TRF showed a response at around 260–300 ms (p < 0.05, one-sided t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical testing.

claim: The 1st-to-2nd cross-correlation coefficient at a temporal lag of around –170 ms was significant.
source: As shown in Figure 3E (top panel), the 1st-to-2nd cross-correlation coefficient at a temporal lag of around –170 ms was significant (permutation test, p < 0.05, corrected), supporting that the 2nd item alpha-band activations essentially preceded those of the 1st item (i.e., negative temporal lag) by around 170 ms.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and statistical testing.

claim: The two items in the memory list are organized into a recurring temporal chunk of approximately 400 ms.
source: This suggests that the two items in the memory list are further organized into a recurring temporal chunk of approximately 400 ms, within which sequentially memorized items reactivate one after another in a reversed order.
evidence: This claim is supported by autocorrelation analysis of experimental data.

claim: The stronger the alpha-band memory effects (i.e., Alpha WM > Alpha NWM), the better the corresponding memory behavioral performances.
source: Thus, the stronger the alpha-band memory effects (i.e., Alpha WM > Alpha NWM), the better the corresponding memory behavioral performances.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis comparing high- and low-performance groups.

claim: The high-recency group displayed a strong and significant backward-sequential alpha profile.
source: Notably, the 'high-recency' group displayed a strong and significant backward-sequential alpha profile (Figure 4F; permutation test, 1 – 2 cross-correlation coefficient at a lag of −170 ms, p < 0.05, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), whereas the 'low-recency' group displayed weak and nonsignificant sequential responses (Figure 4G; permutation test, 1 – 2 cross-correlation coefficient at lag of −170 ms, p = 0.28; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and statistical testing.

claim: There exists an essential relationship between the backward item-by-item reactivation during maintenance and the subsequent recency effect.
source: Thus, our results support an essential association between the backward sequential reactivations and recency effect in sequence memory behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis comparing high- and low-recency groups.

claim: The target response probability was significantly larger for the 2nd item than for the 1st item in the control study.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, the target response probability was significantly larger for the 2nd item than for the 1st item (df = 10, one-tail paired t-test, t = 2.052, p = 0.034, CI: [−0.003, 0.083], Cohen's d = 0.618), confirming the recency effect and excluding the response bias interpretation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the control study and statistical testing.

claim: Memory reactivations during the rehearsal period are compressed in time.
source: Memory reactivations during the rehearsal period are compressed in time, in agreement with previous neurophysiological recordings in animals (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Euston et al., 2007; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Skaggs et al., 1996; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and consistent with previous animal studies.

claim: Discrete epochs of events that are temporally separated in the external world can be successfully associated in the brain within an appropriate time frame, which could be vital for operation of the neuronal plasticity mechanism.
source: Discrete epochs of events that are temporally separated in the external world can be successfully associated in the brain within an appropriate time frame, which could be vital for operation of the neuronal plasticity mechanism (Jensen and Lisman, 2005; Nabavi et al., 2014), and a similar time compression mechanism could mediate sequence maintenance in working memory.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the data and previous literature.

claim: Alpha-band neuronal activities have a key function in working memory by efficiently suppressing distracting information.
source: It is well acknowledged that alpha-band neuronal activities have a key function in working memory by efficiently suppressing distracting information (Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Increased memory load is associated with enhanced alpha-band activities.
source: For instance, increased memory load is associated with enhanced alpha-band activities (Jensen et al., 2002; Klimesch et al., 1999; Tuladhar et al., 2007), and repeated transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) at alpha frequency modulates the short-term memory capacity (Sauseng et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The memory-related alpha response reflects memory reactivations rather than inhibition.
source: Taken together, we reason that the memory-related alpha response in our results reflects memory reactivations rather than inhibition, based on several facts.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: The alpha-band activity in TRF responses might represent the stimulus-induced phase resetting of the intrinsic alpha-band oscillation in EEG activities.
source: We propose that the alpha-band activity in TRF responses might represent the stimulus-induced phase resetting of the intrinsic alpha-band oscillation in EEG activities (Makeig et al., 2002), given their close associations (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the data and previous literature.

claim: Sequence order information is represented and consolidated in short-term memory by an item-by-item serial reactivation mechanism.
source: In conclusion, our results provide converging evidence that sequence order information is represented and consolidated in short-term memory by an item-by-item serial reactivation mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The serial reactivation is temporally compressed within a 200 – 400 ms window and reversed in temporal order.
source: Crucially, the serial reactivation, temporally compressed (i.e., within a 200 – 400 ms window) and reversed in temporal order (i.e., backward reactivation), is essentially associated with the subsequent memory behavioral performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: Fast-backward replay during maintenance might constitute a general neural mechanism for sequence memory and learning.
source: This fast-backward replay during maintenance, previously revealed in rat hippocampus for spatial navigation and shown here in humans for a non-spatial task, might therefore constitute a general neural mechanism for sequence memory and learning.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on convergence of findings from animal and human studies.

claim: Participants maintained good fixation on the central cross (within 1°) throughout each trial.
source: Results showed that the participants maintained good fixation on the central cross (within 1°) throughout each trial (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by eye-tracking data.

claim: The TRF approach is a robust and conservative way to assess the neural response to luminance change.
source: In fact, the TRF approach is quite a robust and conservative way to assess the neural response to luminance change.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the TRF method.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated that applying a quadratic extension of the linear TRF approach only resulted in slight improvement compared to a linear model.
source: Previous studies have also demonstrated that applying a quadratic extension of the linear TRF approach only resulted in slight improvement compared to a linear model (Lalor et al., 2008; Power et al., 2011), further advocating the linear assumption in TRF calculation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Reliable estimation of TRF response requires neural signals with enough temporal length as well as the corresponding length of stimulus sequences.
source: Reliable estimation of TRF response requires neural signals with enough temporal length as well as the corresponding length of stimulus sequences, from which the TRF response characterizing their linear relationship could be calculated.
evidence: This claim is based on established methodological knowledge about TRF analysis.

claim: Neural signals of at least 120 s are needed to obtain TRF responses with reasonable SNR.
source: Previous study has proposed that neural signals of at least 120 s are needed to obtain TRF responses with reasonable SNR (Handy, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The backward reactivation profile is directly related to the subsequent recency effect in memory behavioral performance.
source: Most importantly, this backward reactivation profile is directly related to the subsequent recency effect in memory behavioral performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing high- and low-recency groups.

claim: The sequential replay displays two interesting properties compared to the actual sequence: reversal in order and compression in time.
source: The sequential replay displays two interesting properties compared to the actual sequence. First, the item-by-item reactivation is compressed within a 200 – 400 ms window, suggesting that external events are associated within a plasticity-relevant window to facilitate memory consolidation. Second, the replay is in a temporally reversed order and is strongly related to the recency effect in behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: External events are associated within a plasticity-relevant window to facilitate memory consolidation.
source: First, the item-by-item reactivation is compressed within a 200 – 400 ms window, suggesting that external events are associated within a plasticity-relevant window to facilitate memory consolidation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed temporal compression and knowledge about neuronal plasticity.

claim: The temporal phase patterns of the neural activities during memory retrieval are similar to that during memory encoding.
source: By asking subjects to mentally replay short sound or video clips, the temporal phase patterns of the neural activities during memory retrieval are found to be similar to that during memory encoding, further advocating preservation of temporal information of the stimulus in working memory (Michelmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Working memory contents have been suggested to be maintained in rapid transition in dynamic hidden states.
source: Working memory contents have also been suggested to be maintained in rapid transition in dynamic hidden states (Stokes, 2015; Wolff et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It remains unknown how the human brain represents and maintains temporal order information during the memory retention period, when the stimulus sequence is not present.
source: However, it remains unknown how the human brain represents and maintains temporal order information during the memory retention period, when the stimulus sequence is not present.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Human studies have provided more limited access to the item-specific reactivation profiles at the neuronal ensemble level compared to rodent studies.
source: In contrast to rodent studies in which sequential trajectory of place cell firing could be explicitly assessed to explore reactivation profiles during memory maintenance, human studies have provided more limited access to the item-specific reactivation profiles at the neuronal ensemble level.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of methodological capabilities between animal and human studies.

claim: The TRF method can dissociate item-specific neuronal response during the memory retention interval.
source: To overcome this difficulty, in the present study, we employed sequence memory paradigms in combination with a temporal response function (TRF) method (Crosse et al., 2016; Jia et al., 2017; Lalor et al., 2006) to dissociate the item-specific neuronal response during the memory retention interval.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Each item in a memory list, characterized by an alpha-band neural profile, is successively reactivated to mediate the representation and preservation of ordinal information in memory.
source: Our results demonstrate that each item in a memory list, characterized by an alpha-band neural profile, is successively reactivated to mediate the representation and preservation of ordinal information in memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The item-by-item neuronal profile does not simply echo the sequence in the external world but instead displays two intriguing properties compared to the actual stimulus sequence: reversal in order and compression in time.
source: Importantly, this item-by-item neuronal profile does not simply echo the sequence in the external world but instead displays two intriguing properties compared to the actual stimulus sequence: reversal in order and compression in time.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The item that occupies a late position in the list is reactivated earlier.
source: Specifically, the item that occupies a late position in the list is reactivated earlier (e.g., for sequence 1 – 2, the reactivation profile is 2 – 1 in order), and the whole list encompassing all items is compacted within a 200 – 400 ms temporal window.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The whole list encompassing all items is compacted within a 200 – 400 ms temporal window.
source: Specifically, the item that occupies a late position in the list is reactivated earlier (e.g., for sequence 1 – 2, the reactivation profile is 2 – 1 in order), and the whole list encompassing all items is compacted within a 200 – 400 ms temporal window.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The study provides novel neural evidence in humans that the sequence order information is encoded and preserved in a fast and reverse reactivation sequence.
source: Our study provides novel neural evidence in humans that the sequence order information is encoded and preserved in a fast and reverse reactivation sequence.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: Temporally sequenced activations have been reported in several recent human studies.
source: Temporally sequenced activations have also been reported in several recent human studies.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of previous research.

claim: After being trained in a reasoning task that involves selecting a statistically related object path, the brain spontaneously displays a fast successive representation of states.
source: For example, after being trained in a reasoning task that involves selecting a statistically related object path, the brain spontaneously displays a fast successive representation of states (Kurth-Nelson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Flashing only the starting point of a learned sequence would trigger a prediction wave of responses in primary visual cortices.
source: Recently, an fMRI study demonstrated that flashing only the starting point of a learned sequence would trigger a prediction wave of responses in primary visual cortices (Ekman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A MEG study found that the gamma power shifts along the phase of a theta rhythm as more items are added to memory, thus supporting the 'phase coding' model for episodic memory formation.
source: Finally, a MEG study examined the theta-gamma coupling strength as participants were presented with picture sequences, and found that the gamma power shifts along the phase of a theta rhythm as more items are added to memory, thus supporting the 'phase coding' model for episodic memory formation (Heusser et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The current study examined the memory retention period when items were not presented, whereas previous work studied the encoding period when items appeared serially.
source: First, we examined the memory retention period when items were not presented, whereas the previous work studied the encoding period when items appeared serially.
evidence: This claim distinguishes the current study from previous work.

claim: The current study demonstrates backward reactivations whereas previous study supports a forward-playing profile.
source: Second, we demonstrate backward reactivations whereas the previous study supports a forward-playing profile, further suggesting a fundamental distinction between memory encoding and retention.
evidence: This claim distinguishes the current study from previous work.

claim: Previous neurophysiological recordings in monkeys have revealed forward serial activations in prefrontal population activity.
source: Previous neurophysiological recordings in monkeys have revealed forward serial activations in prefrontal population activity (Siegel et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Sequences within the hippocampus in rats have been observed in both forward and reverse order.
source: Sequences within the hippocampus in rats have been observed in both forward and reverse order (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Louie and Wilson, 2001; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996), and interestingly, the backward sequence has been shown during awake periods immediately after spatial experience (Foster and Wilson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The backward sequence has been shown during awake periods immediately after spatial experience in rats.
source: Sequences within the hippocampus in rats have been observed in both forward and reverse order (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Louie and Wilson, 2001; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996), and interestingly, the backward sequence has been shown during awake periods immediately after spatial experience (Foster and Wilson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A recent MEG work found a backward trajectory of representations of states during a reasoning task.
source: A recent MEG work found a backward trajectory of representations of states (Kurth-Nelson et al., 2016) during a reasoning task.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A reinforcement learning model proposes that the recent item would be the starting and anchoring point for propagating information backward along incoming trajectories to build a recency-weighted running average of the rewards received for each action taken.
source: One interpretation comes from a reinforcement learning model, which proposes that the recent item would be the starting and anchoring point for propagating information backward along incoming trajectories to build a recency-weighted running average of the rewards received for each action taken (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Bornstein et al., 2017; Gershman and Daw, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: The 'activity-silent' model proposes that the contents of working memory are mediated by dynamic hidden states.
source: Another interesting possibility is derived from the 'activity-silent' model (Stokes, 2015), which proposes that the contents of working memory are mediated by dynamic hidden states.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a theoretical model.

claim: Memory-related hidden states could be pinged and inferred out during maintenance in the absence of attention and lingering delay activity.
source: These memory-related hidden states could be pinged and inferred out during maintenance in the absence of attention and lingering delay activity (Wolff et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The TRF response could be regarded as the emerging item-specific activation after each pinging.
source: In our experiments, the TRF response could be regarded as the emerging item-specific activation after each pinging (i.e., each unit luminance transient in the probe stimulus).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the TRF response in the context of the activity-silent model.

claim: The item associated with stronger excitability (i.e., the recent item) would appear with shorter latency compared to the item associated with weaker excitability (i.e., the early item), resulting in reversed sequential reactivation.
source: Consequently, the item associated with stronger excitability (i.e., the recent item) would appear with shorter latency compared to the item associated with weaker excitability (i.e., the early item), resulting in reversed sequential reactivation as we observed here.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed backward reactivation.

claim: How the sequence is presented (sequential or simultaneous) could be another factor accounting for the order of reactivations.
source: How the sequence is presented (sequential or simultaneous) could be another factor accounting for the order of reactivations.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about factors that might influence reactivation order.

claim: Reorganization of events with regard to the internal temporal framework, presumably mediated by neuronal oscillations of various rhythms, may contribute to memory consolidation.
source: Reorganization of events with regard to the internal temporal framework, presumably mediated by neuronal oscillations of various rhythms (e.g., theta, alpha, gamma, etc.), may contribute to memory consolidation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the role of temporal reorganization in memory consolidation.

claim: A recent EEG study revealed that attention samples multiple visual objects in a temporally sequential manner even when subjects maintained sustained attention on one object.
source: A recent EEG study revealed that attention samples multiple visual objects in a temporally sequential manner even when subjects maintained sustained attention on one object (Jia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Sequential attentional sampling could not account for the present observations.
source: We would argue that sequential attentional sampling could not account for the present observations.
evidence: This claim is based on reasoning about the experimental design and results.

claim: All items in the sequence should be attended to with the same priority and thus would not be sequentially sampled by attention.
source: First, a previous study showed that attention would first sample the item associated with highest attentional priority and then would shift to an item associated with less attentional priority. However, here, all items in the sequence should be attended to with the same priority and thus would not be sequentially sampled by attention.
evidence: This claim is based on reasoning about the experimental design.

claim: A previous sequential pattern (attended before unattended) could not reasonably account for the backward reactivation.
source: Second, a previous sequential pattern (attended before unattended) could not reasonably account for the backward reactivation.
evidence: This claim is based on reasoning about the observed results.

claim: Alpha-band neuronal oscillations have recently been found to implement an ''echo'' or reverberation of the inputs.
source: In addition to the traditionally posited inhibitory function in many cognitive processes (Sauseng et al., 2009; Bonnefond and Jensen, 2012; Klimesch, 2012; Händel et al., 2011), alpha-band neuronal oscillations have recently been found to implement an ''echo'' or reverberation of the inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by knowledge of previous research.

claim: Alpha echoes are enhanced by visual attention, supporting an additional role of the alpha-band rhythm in the maintenance of sensory representations over time.
source: These alpha echoes are indeed enhanced by visual attention, supporting an additional role of the alpha-band rhythm in the maintenance of sensory representations over time (VanRullen and Macdonald, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Previous studies using a TRF approach have revealed enhancement in alpha-echoes under attended conditions.
source: First, previous studies using a TRF approach have revealed enhancement in alpha-echoes under attended conditions (Jia et al., 2017; VanRullen and Macdonald, 2012), which could not be interpreted by inhibitory account.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The memory-related alpha responses did not show spatial attention effects.
source: Second, the memory-related alpha responses did not show spatial attention effects (see Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), which are known to be mediated by inhibitory alpha activities (Worden et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: WM showed stronger alpha responses than NWM and were strongly associated with memory behavior.
source: Finally, WM showed stronger alpha responses than NWM here and were strongly associated with memory behavior, further excluding the inhibitory interpretation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and had no history of psychiatric or neurological disorders.
source: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and had no history of psychiatric or neurological disorders.
evidence: This is a description of participant inclusion criteria.

claim: All experiments were carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: All experiments were carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: All participants provided written informed consent prior to the start of the experiment, which was approved by the Research Ethics Committee at Peking University.
source: All participants provided written informed consent prior to the start of the experiment, which was approved by the Research Ethics Committee at Peking University (2015-03-05c2).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: Two subjects in Experiment 1, and one subject in Experiment 2 were excluded because of overall low behavioral performance, excessive eye movements, or not finishing the whole experiment.
source: During data collection and preprocessing, two subjects in Experiment 1, and one subject in Experiment 2 were excluded because of overall low behavioral performance, excessive eye movements, or not finishing the whole experiment.
evidence: This is a description of data exclusion criteria.

claim: The TRF approach has been used to assess brain response that tracks ongoing changes in sound envelope, visual luminance, and even high-level properties.
